name: The helot system
plain_explanation: The native population conquered by the Spartans was reduced to serfs (helots) bound permanently to the land, forced to hand over most of their produce, and periodically terrorized or killed to prevent rebellion.
precise_definition: A hereditary, state-owned serf class attached to Spartan land-lots, unable to be bought or sold individually but not free, subject to an annual declaration of war permitting Spartan youths to kill suspected troublemakers without legal guilt.
why_it_mattered: The entire leisure and 'equality' enjoyed by Spartan citizens rested on this system of forced labor and violence, a fact Russell insists on stating plainly against the romanticized myth.
historical_origin: Established after the Dorian conquest of Laconia and expanded after the conquest of Messenia.
examples: The secret annual 'declaration of war' on the helots, allowing killing without legal penalty.
Plutarch's own discomfort with this practice, which he refuses to attribute to the (in his view) gentle and just Lycurgus.
objections: Plutarch's attempt to exempt Lycurgus personally from responsibility for helot-killing is, in Russell's presentation, an example of the myth softening an otherwise brutal reality.
